query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Using in-situ substrate preheating during laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi alloy reduces compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, thereby improving its overall mechanical integrity relative to conventionally fabricated samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high‐entropy alloy powder that, when processed by conventional L-PBF without temperature control, typically exhibits compositional segregation, high residual thermal stresses, and defect formation.
generation.intervention: Implement in-situ substrate preheating (approximately 500°C) during L-PBF processing.
generation.conditions: L-PBF processing in an inert atmosphere with a build plate maintained at ~500°C, using standard laser parameters; the intervention applies to as-fabricated samples without additional post-processing heat treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: A moderated cooling rate that leads to a more homogeneous elemental distribution, refined microstructure, and tempered thermal gradients, which collectively reduce the density of residual stresses and defects.
generation.mechanism: Substrate preheating reduces the temperature differential between the molten pool and the substrate, decreasing the cooling rate. This slower cooling allows for enhanced element diffusion, limits compositional segregation at dendritic boundaries, reduces the formation of high thermal gradients (which are otherwise responsible for residual stresses) and mitigates defect nucleation (such as cracks and porosity).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to samples fabricated without preheating, samples with substrate preheating are expected to exhibit lower residual stress levels, reduced compositional segregation as evidenced by more uniform microstructures, fewer process-induced defects, and improved mechanical properties (such as increased yield strength and ductility).
generation.baseline: Conventional L-PBF fabricated AlCrFeNiSi samples produced without substrate preheating, which typically show significant segregation, high residual stresses, and a higher defect density.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for as-fabricated L-PBF components of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi processed under controlled inert atmosphere conditions with a substrate preheating temperature around 500°C; effects under different geometries, post-processing treatments, or non-L-PBF methods may vary.
generation.uncertainty: While prior analogous studies support the benefits of thermal gradient moderation in similar HEAs, the exact magnitude of mechanical improvement and segregation reduction in AlCrFeNiSi under these conditions remains to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi samples using L-PBF under identical laser power, scan speed, and inert atmosphere conditions. One set is processed with in-situ substrate preheating at ~500°C, and the other is processed without preheating. Perform a comparative study of their microstructural homogeneity, residual stress levels, defect density, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Microstructural characterization using SEM/EBSD and EDS mapping to assess segregation
Residual stress measurement via XRD analysis
Defect density evaluation through high-resolution microscopy
Mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness measurements) to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed with substrate preheating do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in microstructural homogeneity, lower residual stresses, reduced defect densities, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to those processed without preheating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. Brif et al. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. However, the thermal cycling and partial remelting experienced by previous layers can significantly increase the hot cracking susceptibility of superalloys [].

Fabrication of engineering parts from high-entropy alloys (HEA) using additive manufacturing (AM) has been increasingly studied in the past five years. Initial studies focused on powder bed fusion of CoCrFeNi, a prototype single-phase high entropy alloy with face-centered-cubic (fcc) structure, from pre-alloyed powders, and observed increased strength and ductility compared to cast alloys. Later, the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni system was predominantly studied, either as equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi or as AlxCoCrFeNi with 0.1 < x < 1. Other work demonstrated AM of CoCrFeMnNi by selective laser melting, Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.5Mo0.1 by directed energy deposition, ZrTiVCrFeNi by electron beam melting, and polymer-AlCoCrFeNi composites by coating 260 nm thick 3D printed polymer nanolattices with 14–126 nm thick HEA shells. It is typically observed that AM processing through the liquid state, followed by solidification at high cooling rates, refines the grain size, leads to finer precipitates in two-phase alloys, and produces a highly textured microstructure; however, it may require high preheating temperatures to attenuate cracking, and it leads to inter-dendritic segregation of elements and microstructural g

Additive manufacturing (AM) techniques have broadened many aspects of component design, enabled part count reduction, and decreased commissioning time for prospective NASA hardware and industrial applications. Currently, the bulk of metallic AM research has been conducted on traditional alloys. Yet, AM facilitates new avenues for materials discovery that have not been fully explored,. For laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), the finely focused, laser melting of powder is analogous to welding and is thus problematic for alloys that are difficult to weld. Unfortunately, many of the alloys used for ultra-high temperature applications (>1000 °C) fall within this criterion. Therefore, there currently exists a need for high temperature alloys that can be produced through L-PBF or similar AM processes. One alloy system that has shown promise is the multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) class. The discovery and growth of this interesting new class of alloys, coined “High Entropy alloys”, has coincided with the development of AM.
